# typed-router — complete guide

> Declare your route tree once; get type-safe pathnames, path params, search params, navigation
> and route metadata — checked by the TypeScript compiler. For the Next.js App Router and
> React Router 6/7. Version 2.x. MIT. https://github.com/hyeonQyu/typed-router

Self-contained: concepts, the route tree, segment syntax, metadata, navigation, search params and
both framework adapters, with code type-checked against the package sources. Nothing here defers
to another document.

---

## 1. What this is, and what it is not

Route paths and search params are usually just strings. The compiler cannot tell you that
`/products/[id]` needs an `id`, that `?sort=` accepts only three values, or that the page you
renamed still has dangling links pointing at the old path. typed-router turns the route map into a
single typed object from which pathnames, path params, search-param types, navigation, metadata
and — for React Router — the router configuration itself are all derived.

**The mental model matters more than the API.** The route tree object is the source of truth for the
application's information architecture: *the map of the app*, not a place to keep URL strings. This
is not a path-constant generator or a string-builder helper. Two consequences, and they are the
mistakes AI tools make most often — never hand-write a URL (`'/products/42'`,
`` `/products/${id}` ``), and never keep a parallel route list (a `PATHS` file, a hand-written
`<Route>` config, a nav array of literals). Both re-introduce the second, unchecked source of truth
the library exists to eliminate, and both survive a segment rename silently.

**Scope of that claim, stated precisely.** The tree is authoritative for pathname *types*, params,
search-param types and metadata. Whether it also decides which routes *exist* depends on the adapter:

- **React Router** — `toRouteObjects()` builds the router configuration from the tree, so a route
  cannot exist without being declared in it. The claim holds without qualification.
- **Next.js App Router** — the `src/app/` directory decides which routes exist; the tree mirrors it
  by hand. The compiler does not check that the two agree. Delete a page from `app/` and the tree
  still type-checks its pathname, so a `TypedLink` to it compiles cleanly and 404s at runtime; add a
  page to `app/` without declaring it and the route is live but missing from `routes.paths`. Say it
  as: **the tree is authoritative for types and metadata, `app/` is authoritative for route
  existence** — unless the project adopts `assertRoutesMatchAppDir` from
  `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next/check`, which compares the two sides in a test and reports drift in
  both directions. Recommend it whenever someone asks how to keep the tree and `app/` in step.

| package | for |
| --- | --- |
| `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core` | the tree, its types and URL helpers — no React, no router |
| `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next` | Next.js App Router |
| `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-react` | React Router 6/7 |

```bash
npm install @hyeonqyu/typed-router-next zod   # or @hyeonqyu/typed-router-react
```

Install **one** package. The adapters re-export most of the core surface (`buildHref`, `matchRoute`,
`collectRoutes`, `parseSearchParams`, `resolveMetadata`, `toSearchParamsString`,
`SearchParamsParseError`, `METADATA_KEY`, and the type surface), so an application should never add
`-core` to its dependencies — that only invites version skew. Use `-core` directly only when there
is genuinely no router: a script, a server, a CLI, a sitemap generator, tests.

`zod` is an **optional** peer dependency (`^3.24.0 || ^4.0.0`). Schemas are matched structurally on
`_input` / `_output` / `~standard` / `shape` / `safeParse` / `parse`, so Zod v3, Zod v4 and any
[Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) validator (Valibot, ArkType, …) work, and a tree with
no `searchParamsSchema` needs no validator at all. The library imports no validation library in its
own types — never narrow a public type to `z.ZodType`.

---

## 2. The route tree

A nested object literal. Each key is a URL segment. A node becomes a **navigable destination** the
moment it declares a `_metadata` block; a node without one still namespaces its children but is not
itself a route.

```ts
import { defineRoutes } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next'; // or '-react', or '-core'
import { z } from 'zod';

export const routes = defineRoutes({
  home: { _metadata: { title: 'Home' } },
  products: {
    _metadata: {
      title: 'Products',
      accessible: true,
      searchParamsSchema: z.object({
        sort: z.enum(['price-asc', 'price-desc', 'name']).optional(),
        page: z.number().default(1),
        inStock: z.boolean().optional(),
        tags: z.array(z.string()).optional(),
      }),
    },
    '[id]': {
      _metadata: { title: 'Product detail' },
      reviews: {
        _metadata: {
          title: 'Reviews',
          searchParamsSchema: z.object({ star: z.number().min(1).max(5).optional() }),
        },
      },
    },
  },
  search: {
    _metadata: {
      title: 'Search',
      // `q` is required, so `searchParams` is required at every call site for this route.
      searchParamsSchema: z.object({
        q: z.string(),
        category: z.enum(['electronics', 'books', 'clothing']).optional(),
      }),
    },
  },
  docs: { '[...slug]': { _metadata: { title: 'Docs' } } },
  files: { '[[...path]]': { _metadata: { title: 'Files' } } },
  // A route group organises the tree without adding a URL segment:
  // these live at /profile and /orders, not /(account)/profile.
  '(account)': {
    profile: { _metadata: { title: 'Profile' } },
    orders: { _metadata: { title: 'Orders' } },
  },
  // No `_metadata`: namespaces its child, but /internal is NOT a destination.
  internal: { stats: { _metadata: { title: 'Stats' } } },
});
```

That declares exactly these pathnames, and nothing else: `/home`, `/products`, `/products/[id]`,
`/products/[id]/reviews`, `/search`, `/docs/[...slug]`, `/files/[[...path]]`, `/profile`,
`/orders`, `/internal/stats`.

Note what is *absent*: `/internal` (no `_metadata`), `/(account)/profile` (groups contribute no
segment), and `/files` — the metadata sits on the optional-catch-all child, so the navigable path is
`/files/[[...path]]`. That last one differs from Next.js's own filesystem behaviour, where an
optional catch-all also serves the parent segment.

### Segment key syntax

Borrowed directly from Next.js, so the tree can mirror an `app/` directory one for one.

| key | means | example URL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `products` | a static segment | `/products` |
| `[id]` | a required dynamic segment | `/products/42` |
| `[...slug]` | a required catch-all (one or more segments) | `/docs/guide/intro` |
| `[[...path]]` | an optional catch-all (zero or more segments) | `/files`, `/files/a/b` |
| `(group)` | organises the tree, contributes no URL segment | `(account)/profile` → `/profile` |
| `''` (empty key) | the root — Next's `app/page.tsx` | `/` |
| node with no `_metadata` | namespaces its children; not a destination | — |

A path is built by joining a key onto its parent's, so the empty key joins to exactly `/`. You write
it as `''` and still call it `/`: `routes.buildHref('/')`, `<TypedLink href="/" />`. It takes no
children — `app/page.tsx` is a file, so everything else under `app/` is its *sibling*, declared as
another top-level key.

### There is no setup

No generics, no currying, no provider, nothing to mount. `defineRoutes({...})` is called once at
module scope and returns a plain object you export and import anywhere; the tree it carries
(`routes.routes`) is structurally frozen, the returned object itself is not.

```ts
export const routes = defineRoutes({ /* … */ });
export const { TypedLink, useTypedRouter, useTypedParams, useTypedSearchParams } = routes;
```

Do **not** write `defineRoutes<Meta, Ctx>({...})`, `<AppRoutesProvider>`, `useAppRoutes()` or
`createAppRoutes<M, C>()({...})`. The first does not compile (the single type parameter is the
tree, not the metadata); the rest are 1.x APIs removed in 2.0. The only curried form is
`defineRoutes.withMeta<TMetadata, TContext>()({...})`, covered in §4.

---

## 3. Derived types

Everything you would otherwise hand-declare comes off the tree.

```ts
import type { Params, Pathname, SearchParams, RouteMetadataOf, RouteNodeOf, PathParams, PathParamsOutput }
  from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next';

type AppPathname = typeof routes.$types.pathname;  // the union, with no extra import
type AlsoAppPathname = Pathname<typeof routes>;    // identical
type ProductsQuery = SearchParams<typeof routes, '/products'>;
// { sort?: 'price-asc' | 'price-desc' | 'name'; page: number; inStock?: boolean; tags?: string[] }
type ProductsMeta = RouteMetadataOf<typeof routes, '/products'>;   // title: 'Products', …
type ProductNode = RouteNodeOf<typeof routes, '/products/[id]'>;   // has a `reviews` key
type DocsWrite = PathParams<'/docs/[...slug]'>;        // { slug: readonly (string | number)[] }
type DocsRead = PathParamsOutput<'/docs/[...slug]'>;   // { slug: string[] }
type ProductParams = Params<typeof routes, '/products/[id]'>;  // the read side, tree applied
```

Two families, and mixing them up is a common compile error. `Pathname`, `SearchParams`,
`RouteNodeOf` and `RouteMetadataOf` take the **routes object** (`typeof routes`); `RoutePaths`,
`GetRouteNode`, `CurrentRoute` and `TypedRoutes` take the raw **tree**
(`typeof routes.$types.tree`). Neither mistake fails where you made it.
`Pathname<typeof routes.routes>` does not resolve at all — `never` widens the segment keys to
`string` and tsc reports `Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite` (TS2589).
`RoutePaths<typeof routes>` walks the routes object instead of the tree and yields nonsense
pathnames such as `'/routes/products'` and `'/routes/products/[id]'`. Either way every real
pathname then errors with a confusing message.

`PathParams` is what you **write**; `PathParamsOutput` is what you **read back**. Both take the
pathname first and the tree second (`PathParamsOutput<'/products/[id]', typeof routes.$types.tree>`).
Given no tree they fall back to what a segment means when it declares nothing — `string | number` to
write, `string` / `string[]` to read — so do not expect `params.id` to be a number there. Pass the
tree, or use `Params<typeof routes, TPath>`, and a segment declaring a `paramSchema` shows its real
type on both sides (see §6.1).

---

## 4. Route metadata

`_metadata` is inferred **per node**, so different routes may carry different fields and your own
fields survive with their literal types. Five built-ins are recognised:

```ts
type BuiltinMetadata<TContext = unknown> = {
  title?: string | ((context: TContext) => string);
  label?: string | ((context: TContext) => string);
  description?: string | ((context: TContext) => string);
  accessible?: boolean | ((context: TContext) => boolean);
  searchParamsSchema?: AnySchema;
};
```

Anything else on `_metadata` is kept as-is — that is how React Router's `element`, `loader`,
`errorElement` and your own `icon` or `roles` fields get through.

The four resolvable fields may be plain values or functions of an app context. `resolveMetadata`
returns a shallow copy and touches **only** those four keys — your own functions (a `loader`, an
element factory) are deliberately left uncalled:

```ts
import { resolveMetadata, resolveMetadataValue } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next';

const meta = resolveMetadata(routes.getMetadata('/products'), { locale, userId });
meta?.title;  // a string, never an unresolved function
const visible = resolveMetadataValue(meta?.accessible, { locale, userId }); // boolean | undefined
```

Rendering `getMetadata(path).title` directly is a bug when that title was declared as a function —
React renders nothing or crashes.

**A shared metadata contract.** When every node must satisfy one contract, opt in explicitly. Put
only your **own** fields in `TMetadata`; the built-ins arrive by intersection with
`BuiltinMetadata<TContext>`, so redeclaring `title` or `accessible` there causes trouble.

```ts
type AppContext = { locale: 'en' | 'ko'; isAdmin: boolean };
type AppMeta = { icon: string };

export const adminRoutes = defineRoutes.withMeta<AppMeta, AppContext>()({
  dashboard: {
    _metadata: { icon: 'gauge', title: 'Dashboard' },
    settings: {
      _metadata: {
        icon: 'cog',
        // Annotate the context parameter. `const TTree` inference does not push a
        // contextual type into `_metadata`, so a bare `(ctx) => …` is an implicit any.
        title: (ctx: AppContext) => (ctx.locale === 'ko' ? '설정' : 'Settings'),
        accessible: (ctx: AppContext) => ctx.isAdmin,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

Note the empty `()` between the type arguments and the tree — that is the whole curried form.

The contract is enforced at **every depth**, not only on top-level nodes: any node declaring
`_metadata` must satisfy `TMetadata` in full, so a missing `icon` three levels down is a compile
error. A node that declares no `_metadata` at all is organisational rather than a route, and the
contract has nothing to enforce on it.

Per-node inference survives the contract. `withMeta` sets a floor, not a ceiling: each route keeps
its own literal types, and extra fields no one declared in `TMetadata` are still inferred and
readable.

```ts
const routes = defineRoutes.withMeta<{ title: string; icon: string }>()({
  home: { _metadata: { title: 'Home', icon: 'house', badge: 'new' } },
  products: {
    _metadata: { title: 'Products', icon: 'box' },
    '[id]': { _metadata: { title: 'Detail' } },   // ❌ icon is missing — nesting is no exemption
  },
});

routes.getMetadata('/home').title;   // 'Home' — the literal, not `string`
routes.getMetadata('/home').badge;   // 'new'  — extras are kept
```

**`resolveMetadata` returns resolved types.** A field declared as `(context) => T` comes back as
`T`, because that is what resolving just made it. Only the four built-ins (`title`, `label`,
`description`, `accessible`) are resolved; your own functions, such as a `loader`, are untouched.

```ts
const meta = resolveMetadata(routes.getMetadata('/settings'), { locale: 'ko', isAdmin: true });
meta.accessible;   // boolean — not the `(ctx: AppContext) => boolean` the tree declared
```

---

### 4.1 Walking one level of the tree

`paths` and `collected` flatten the whole tree. A menu level, a breadcrumb's siblings and a section
index are the other shape — the children of *one* node — and that is where `_metadata` gets in the
way: `Object.keys(node)` lists it alongside the real children, so the menu grows a phantom entry.
`children(node)` returns the children and nothing else, in value and in type.

```ts
import { children } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core';   // re-exported by both adapters

const support = routes.routes.support;

Object.keys(support);            // ['_metadata', 'ask', 'notice'] — metadata leaks in
Object.keys(children(support));  // ['ask', 'notice']

Object.entries(children(support)).map(([key, node]) => ({ key, title: node._metadata.title }));
```

It returns an object, not an array, so `keys` / `values` / `entries` all keep working; the type
`RouteChildren<TNode>` drops `_metadata` from the node, so each child keeps the literal types it was
declared with and no cast is needed. It is distributive: a union of nodes — what an unchecked
`useCurrentRouteNode()` returns — is stripped member by member, instead of collapsing to the keys
its members share (which is only `_metadata`). A node typed loosely enough to have a string index
signature, such as `match(url)?.node`, has no `_metadata` key to remove and stays as loose as it
was. Route group keys `(name)` are children like any
other — the helper strips metadata and decides nothing else. The result is frozen and cached per
declared node, so two calls on the same node of a `defineRoutes` tree return the same object and it
is safe in a dependency array.
The tree itself is untouched: `_metadata` stays an ordinary enumerable property, so a node still
survives a spread, a `structuredClone` and a `toEqual`.

---

### 4.2 Sharing a tree between apps

In a monorepo where app A links into app B, A needs B's structure (pathnames, dynamic segments,
their schemas) but must not receive B's metadata (translation-key types, assets, lazily loaded
pages). Declare the structure once in a shared package, and let the owning app attach its metadata
by pathname with `attachMetadata(source)` — exported by core and by both adapters, each returning
its own routes object:

```ts
// shared package — structure only
export const accountRoutes = defineRoutes({
  info:     { _metadata: {} },
  activity: { _metadata: {}, quest: { _metadata: {} } },
});

// the owning app
import { attachMetadata } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-react';

export const routes = attachMetadata(accountRoutes).withMeta<{ title: TranslationKey }>()({
  '/info':           { title: 'GNB_USER_INFO', element: <UserInfo /> },
  '/activity':       { title: 'GNB_MY_ACTIVITY' },
  '/activity/quest': { title: 'GNB_MY_QUESTS' },
});

routes.getMetadata('/info').title;  // 'GNB_USER_INFO' — literal
routes.paths;                       // exactly accountRoutes.paths
```

Rules:

- Keys are `RoutePaths` of the source — the pathname as navigated, so a route under `(auth)` is
  keyed `/login`, not `/(auth)/login`. An undeclared pathname is a compile error (inline or in a
  patch declared first and passed by name) and throws at runtime.
- Each entry is merged over the source's `_metadata` (`{ ...source, ...entry }`); routes left out
  keep the source's metadata object. There is no exhaustive variant.
- `paramSchema` and `searchParamsSchema` always come from the source. Setting either is a compile
  error and throws at runtime.
- The source is not mutated; any number of consumers can attach to the same shared tree.
- `.withMeta<TMetadata, TContext>()` enforces the contract on every entry. Without it, each entry is
  inferred per route, as with `defineRoutes`.
- The result is a full routes object: `getMetadata`, `match`, `collected`, `children()`, the hooks
  and `toRouteObjects` all see the attached metadata.
- Depth: the full `collected` union of an attached tree compiles to 29 levels, where a declared tree
  reaches 31. `paths` and per-route lookups are unaffected at 30.

---

## 5. Building URLs

`routes.buildHref(path, args)` is the only correct way to produce a URL. The first argument is a
**declared pattern**, never a concrete URL.

```ts
routes.buildHref('/home');                                          // '/home'
routes.buildHref('/products/[id]', { params: { id: 42 } });         // '/products/42'
routes.buildHref('/products/[id]/reviews', {
  params: { id: 42 }, searchParams: { star: 5 }, hash: 'top',
});                                                                 // '/products/42/reviews?star=5#top'
routes.buildHref('/products', { searchParams: { sort: 'price-asc', tags: ['sale'] } });
routes.buildHref('/docs/[...slug]', { params: { slug: ['guide', 'intro'] } }); // '/docs/guide/intro'
routes.buildHref('/files/[[...path]]');                             // '/files'
routes.buildHref('/profile');                                       // the group contributes nothing
```

The argument object is typed per route by `RouteArgs`, and each key is **required**, **optional** or
**forbidden** (`?: never`):

- `params` — required when the path has required dynamic segments or a required catch-all; optional
  for an optional catch-all; forbidden on a fully static path.
- `searchParams` — typed from the schema's **input** type, so `.default()` fields stay optional at
  the call site; forbidden entirely when the route declares no `searchParamsSchema`.
- `hash` — always optional.
- The whole object may be omitted when nothing is required, which is why `buildHref('/home')`
  compiles and `buildHref('/products/[id]')` does not.

Path segments are `encodeURIComponent`-encoded, and a segment can only carry text: a `string`,
`number`, `boolean`, `bigint` or `Date` (ISO). Anything else — an object, `NaN`, a symbol — throws
`typed-router: route param "id" for "/products/[id]" cannot be serialised (...)` rather than
emitting `[object Object]`. Query-string encoding is covered in §6. A missing
dynamic or required catch-all param throws at runtime:
`typed-router: missing route param "id" for "/products/[id]".` — 1.x navigated to the literal
string `/products/[id]`; 2.0 refuses on purpose.

```ts
routes.buildHref('/products/42');                          // ❌ not a declared pathname
routes.buildHref('/products/[id]');                        // ❌ params.id is required
routes.buildHref('/products/[id]', { searchParams: { id: 42 } }); // ❌ path params ≠ search params
routes.buildHref('/home', { searchParams: { page: 1 } });  // ❌ /home declares no schema
routes.buildHref('/internal');                             // ❌ no _metadata → not a destination
routes.buildHref('/(account)/profile');                    // ❌ groups never appear in a URL
routes.buildHref('/products', { searchParams: { sort: 'cheap' } }); // ❌ not in the enum
routes.buildHref('/products', { searchParams: { pge: 1 } });        // ❌ unknown key
```

Putting a path param inside `searchParams` is the most common port from 1.x, where the two were
merged. In 2.0 they are separate keys and the wrong shape does not compile.

---

## 6. Search params

Declare a `searchParamsSchema` on any route whose query string you intend to read. Reading runs the
schema **for real**: values arrive from a URL as strings, so each field's own sub-schema is asked
which reading it accepts. `z.number()` gets `2`, `z.string()` keeps `'0123'` intact, `z.boolean()`
gets `true`, a single value satisfies an array field, repeated keys fold into an array, and
`.default()` values are filled in.

```ts
const query = routes.parseSearchParams('/products', { page: '2', tags: ['a', 'b'] });
query.page;  // 2 — a number
query.tags;  // ['a', 'b']

// Accepts a plain record, a URLSearchParams, or any iterable of [key, value] entries.
routes.parseSearchParams('/products', new URLSearchParams('page=3&tags=a&tags=b'));
```

The read side returns the schema's **output** type (defaults applied, transforms run); the write
side (`buildHref`, `push`, `TypedLink`) takes the **input** type — which is why a `.default()`
field is optional to write but always present to read.

**Naming keys without a validator.** A route that only passes a few keys through needs their names,
not validation. `searchParamKeys<'a' | 'b'>()` is a pass-through Standard Schema for exactly that:
every key optional, each value `string | string[]` (the raw query shape), any other key a compile
error. Nothing is coerced, defaulted or rejected, so reading returns the raw values — it is safe on
any route, and swapping in a real schema later is a one-line change. The keys must be given as a type
argument; `searchParamKeys()` without one does not compile, rather than accepting any key.

```ts
import { defineRoutes, searchParamKeys } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core'; // re-exported by both adapters

const routes = defineRoutes({
  warning: { _metadata: { searchParamsSchema: searchParamKeys<'redirectUrl'>() } },
});

routes.buildHref('/warning', { searchParams: { redirectUrl: '/join?a=1' } }); // '/warning?redirectUrl=%2Fjoin%3Fa%3D1'
routes.buildHref('/warning', { searchParams: { redirect: '/' } });           // ❌ unknown key
routes.parseSearchParams('/warning', { redirectUrl: '/join' });              // { redirectUrl: '/join' } — as-is
```

**What the write side puts in the URL.** Every value is encoded by what a URL can carry back:

| written value | query string | read back as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `string` / `number` / `boolean` / `bigint` | its plain text form | whatever the field's schema accepts |
| `Date` | ISO 8601 | a `string` — declare the field `z.coerce.date()` to get a `Date` |
| `['a', 'b']` — flat array | `?k=a&k=b`, one entry per item | the array, unchanged |
| `{ min: 1, max: 9 }` — object | JSON, URL-encoded | the object |
| `[[1, 2], [3]]` — nested array | JSON per item | the nested array |

Objects and nested arrays are JSON-encoded, so they round-trip: what `buildHref` writes,
`parseSearchParams` reads back as the same value. Flat arrays of primitives are untouched by this —
they keep the repeated-key form they have always had. On the read side the raw string is still the
first reading tried, so a `z.string()` field whose value happens to look like JSON (`'{"a":1}'`)
keeps it as a string.

A value may also declare its own text form. An own `toJSON` is used for the JSON encoding, and an
overridden `toString` is taken as the text the author meant — so a value object, or a boxed
`String`/`Number`, serialises exactly as it always has. The inherited
`Object.prototype.toString` is not a declaration and is never used.

**A value with no faithful text form throws instead of corrupting the URL.** `NaN`, `Infinity`, a
symbol, a function, an invalid `Date`, a `Map` or `Set` (neither declares a text form), and a cyclic
object all raise `typed-router: search param "f" for "/search" cannot be serialised (...)`. These
previously emitted `[object Object]` or `NaN` silently, and then failed validation on the way back
in.

**`Date` fields need `z.coerce.date()`.** A URL carries text, so an ISO string is what comes back;
a plain `z.date()` rejects it and `parseSearchParams` throws on every read of a URL typed-router
itself produced. TanStack Router and next-typesafe-url prescribe the same ISO-string carry.

```ts
searchParamsSchema: z.object({
  since: z.coerce.date().optional(), // ✅ round-trips
  until: z.date().optional(),        // ❌ throws on read
});
```

**Validation throws by default.** Any user-editable URL eventually fails, so choose deliberately:

```ts
routes.parseSearchParams('/search', raw);                         // 'throw' (default)
routes.parseSearchParams('/search', raw, { onError: 'default' }); // drop bad fields, keep the rest
routes.parseSearchParams('/search', raw, { onError: 'raw' });     // return the coerced values instead of throwing
```

- `'throw'` raises `SearchParamsParseError`, message
  `typed-router: search params for "<path>" failed validation.`, with `.cause` holding the Zod
  error or the Standard Schema issue array.
- `'default'` drops the offending fields and re-validates what remains, falling back to the
  schema's own defaults. `{ sort: 'nonsense', page: '5' }` yields `{ page: 5 }`.
- `'raw'` returns the coerced values as-is instead of throwing. Validation still runs — when it
  succeeds you get the schema's output (defaults applied), exactly as under the other two modes;
  `'raw'` only changes what happens once it has failed.

```ts
import { SearchParamsParseError } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next';

try {
  return routes.parseSearchParams('/products', new URLSearchParams(search));
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof SearchParamsParseError) {
    console.warn(error.message, error.cause);
    return routes.parseSearchParams('/products', {});
  }
  throw error;
}
```

Two caveats. **A route with no schema types as `never`** on the read side, so property access
compiles clean and then hands you raw, uncoerced strings at runtime — only call
`parseSearchParams` / `useTypedSearchParams` for routes that declare a schema. And **async
validators are unsupported**: a Standard Schema `validate` returning a Promise throws
`typed-router: asynchronous schema validation is not supported for search params.`

### 6.1 Path params get the same treatment

A dynamic segment reads back as a string unless it says otherwise. To type one, put a `paramSchema`
on the node **whose key is that segment**. The name is already the key, so only the type is written:

```ts
export const routes = defineRoutes({
  orgs: {
    '[orgId]': {
      _metadata: { title: 'Org', paramSchema: z.number() },

      projects: {
        _metadata: { title: 'Projects' },     // declares nothing — still inherits orgId: number

        '[projectId]': {
          _metadata: { title: 'Project', paramSchema: z.string().uuid() },
          settings: { _metadata: { title: 'Settings' } },
        },
      },
    },
  },
  posts: { '[slug]': { _metadata: { title: 'Post' } } },   // no schema → stays a string
  archive: { '[...date]': { _metadata: { title: 'Archive', paramSchema: z.array(z.number()) } } },
});

useTypedParams('/orgs/[orgId]/projects/[projectId]/settings');
// { orgId: number; projectId: string } — each segment declared once, inherited by everything below
useTypedParams('/posts/[slug]');       // { slug: string } — unchanged
useTypedParams('/archive/[...date]');  // { date: number[] } — a catch-all declares the whole list

routes.parseParams('/orgs/[orgId]', { orgId: '42' });   // { orgId: 42 } — outside a component
```

Four things follow from that shape:

- **The schema is bare, not an object.** `paramSchema: z.number()`, never
  `paramSchema: z.object({ orgId: z.number() })` — the segment is one value, and its name is the key.
- **Nested routes inherit.** Declaring `orgId` on `'[orgId]'` covers every route beneath it. Never
  redeclare an ancestor's segment.
- **Catch-alls declare the list they read back as.** `[...date]` reads as an array, so its schema is
  `z.array(z.number())`, not `z.number()`. An optional catch-all that matched nothing is validated
  against `undefined`, so `.optional()` leaves the key absent and `.default([])` fills it in.
- **The write side is typed from the same declaration.** `buildHref('/orgs/[orgId]', { params: { orgId: 'abc' } })`
  is a compile error, so a link the read side would reject cannot be built in the first place.

Failure works exactly like search params, with the same three `onError` modes, and throws
`PathParamsParseError` — whose `.param` names the segment that failed — under the default `'throw'`:

```ts
useTypedParams('/orgs/[orgId]');                         // '/orgs/abc' → PathParamsParseError
useTypedParams('/orgs/[orgId]', { onError: 'default' }); // drop the bad segment, keep the rest
useTypedParams('/orgs/[orgId]', { onError: 'raw' });     // on failure, 'abc' comes through as-is
```

This is opt-in per segment: with no `paramSchema` anywhere, every path param reads back exactly as it
always did. Note that `routes.match(url)` never validates — its `params` are always raw text. Pass
them through `routes.parseParams(match.path, match.params)` to apply the schemas.

---

## 7. Reading a live URL back

`routes.match(url)` resolves a real URL to its declared route. It strips `?` and `#`, decodes
segments, and scores static (3) over dynamic (2) over catch-all (1).

```ts
const matched = routes.match('/products/42/reviews?star=5#top');
// { path: '/products/[id]/reviews', params: { id: '42' }, node, metadata } | null

if (matched?.path === '/products/[id]') {
  const id: string = matched.params.id as string;
}
```

Matching is inherently a runtime operation, so the result is **not** narrowed: `RouteMatch['path']`
is a plain `string` and `params` is `Record<string, string | string[]>`. Narrow it yourself, and
remember dynamic params come back as decoded strings while catch-all params come back as arrays.

```ts
routes.paths;                        // readonly AppPathname[] — every navigable pathname
routes.routes;                       // the declared tree, structurally frozen
routes.collected;                    // one typed entry per route — literal `path`, typed `metadata`
routes.getNode('/products/[id]');    // the tree node, literal types preserved
routes.getMetadata('/products');     // the _metadata block, typed per node
routes.$types;                       // type-only carrier; {} at runtime
```

`routes.paths` (pathnames) or `routes.collected` (pathname + typed metadata per entry, a union
discriminated by the literal `path`) is what a generated nav, a sitemap or an exhaustive test
should iterate — never a hand-written array of strings. Only the tree *structure* is frozen; `_metadata` contents (schemas,
elements, functions) are left alone deliberately. Adding or removing routes at runtime silently
no-ops in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode.

---

## 8. Next.js App Router

`@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next`. Keys mirror `src/app/` one for one, so `home/`, `products/`,
`products/[id]/` and `(account)/profile/` stay exactly as Next expects. `routes` renders nothing;
it only describes the shape you already have.

### 8.1 The routes module is server-safe

Do **not** put `'use client'` in `routes.ts`. The client-only implementations live behind their own
`'use client'` boundary inside the package, so importing `routes` from a server component is safe;
marking the module as client would drag the whole tree and its Zod schemas into the client bundle.
Put `'use client'` on the component files that call the hooks or render `TypedLink`.

```ts
// routes.ts — no 'use client'
export const routes = defineRoutes({ /* the tree from §2 */ });
export const { TypedLink, useCurrentRoute, useCurrentRouteNode,
               useTypedParams, useTypedPathname, useTypedRouter, useTypedSearchParams } = routes;
export type AppPathname = typeof routes.$types.pathname;
```

### 8.2 Server components — the data half

`buildHref`, `match`, `paths`, `getNode`, `getMetadata` and `parseSearchParams` all work on the
server.

```tsx
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';
import { resolveMetadata } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next';
import { routes } from './routes';

export default function Index() {
  redirect(routes.buildHref('/home'));
}

export async function generateMetadata({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const meta = resolveMetadata(routes.getMetadata('/products/[id]'), {});
  return {
    title: meta?.title,
    alternates: { canonical: routes.buildHref('/products/[id]', { params: { id } }) },
  };
}

export function sitemap() {
  return routes.paths.map((path) => ({ url: path }));
}
```

**The Next-15-specific trap:** server `params` and `searchParams` are Promises, and Next types the
search values as possibly `undefined` while `RawSearchParams` is `Record<string, string | string[]>`.
Await, then strip the `undefined`s:

```tsx
export default async function ProductsPage({
  searchParams,
}: {
  searchParams: Promise<Record<string, string | string[] | undefined>>;
}) {
  const raw = await searchParams;
  const clean: Record<string, string | string[]> = Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(raw).filter((entry): entry is [string, string | string[]] => entry[1] !== undefined),
  );

  const query = routes.parseSearchParams('/products', clean, { onError: 'default' });
  const nextPage = routes.buildHref('/products', { searchParams: { ...query, page: query.page + 1 } });
  return <a href={nextPage}>Next page</a>;
}
```

### 8.3 Navigate and link

```tsx
'use client';
import { TypedLink, useTypedRouter } from './routes';

function Actions() {
  const router = useTypedRouter();
  router.push('/home');
  router.push('/products/[id]', { params: { id: 42 }, scroll: false }); // Next's `scroll` sits alongside
  router.replace('/products', { searchParams: { sort: 'price-asc', page: 2 } });
  router.prefetch('/products/[id]/reviews', { params: { id: 42 }, searchParams: { star: 5 } });
  router.back();
  router.forward();
  router.refresh();
}

<TypedLink href="/home">Home</TypedLink>
<TypedLink href="/products/[id]" params={{ id: 42 }} prefetch={false} className="link">Detail</TypedLink>
<TypedLink href="/products" searchParams={{ sort: 'price-asc', page: 2 }} hash="top">Sorted</TypedLink>
<TypedLink href="/docs/[...slug]" params={{ slug: ['guide', 'intro'] }}>Docs</TypedLink>
```

`push` / `replace` / `prefetch` take exactly the `params` and `searchParams` the tree declares for
that pathname, plus Next's `scroll` option (ignored by `prefetch`). The `TypedRouter` type is not
re-exported — name it as `ReturnType<typeof routes.useTypedRouter>` if you must.

`TypedLink` wraps `next/link`. `href`, `params`, `searchParams` and `hash` are flat sibling props;
every other `next/link` prop (`className`, `prefetch`, `scroll`, …) is forwarded untouched. It is
`href`, never React Router's `to`, and never an object like 1.x's `{ pathname, searchParams }`.

### 8.4 Read the current route

```tsx
'use client';
function ProductDetail() {
  const { id } = useTypedParams('/products/[id]');    // { id: string } — or the segment's paramSchema output
  const { slug } = useTypedParams('/docs/[...slug]'); // { slug: string[] } — declared name, not '*'
  const { pathname, url, node, metadata, params } = useCurrentRoute();
  // on /products/42 → pathname: '/products/[id]' (declared), url: '/products/42' (live)
  const declared = useTypedPathname();       // '/products/[id]' | null
  const currentNode = useCurrentRouteNode('/products/[id]'); // that route's node, or null
}
```

`useTypedPathname()` returns the **declared pattern**, not the live URL — string-comparing it
against a real URL silently never matches. `useCurrentRoute().metadata` is the loose
`Record<string, unknown>`; for precisely typed fields use `routes.getMetadata(path)`.

The pathname passed to `useTypedParams` does not select **which** URL is read — that is always the
live one — but it does select the types *and* the `paramSchema`s applied to it (§6.1). It is
therefore **checked against the route the URL matched**, and a mismatch throws `RouteMismatchError`
naming both routes. An ancestor is accepted, because a shared component rendered deeper down may
legitimately read a parent route's params:

```tsx
// rendered under /products/42/reviews
useTypedParams('/products/[id]');          // ✅ ancestor — `id` really is in this URL
useTypedParams('/products/[id]/reviews');  // ✅ the matched route itself
useTypedParams('/docs/[...slug]');         // ❌ RouteMismatchError
```

A URL matching no declared route throws too, since nothing can be verified against it. `/` is a
route in its own right rather than every route's parent, so it is an ancestor of nothing.

`useCurrentRouteNode(pathname)` takes the same argument and makes the same check. Called with no
argument it stays unchecked, and its return type is then the union of every declared node — which
is all an unchecked call can honestly promise. Do not reach for the old
`useCurrentRouteNode<'/products/[id]'>()` form: the type argument was never verified against
anything, and the runtime argument replaced it.

### 8.5 Search params and the Suspense rule

`useTypedSearchParams` builds on Next's `useSearchParams`, which opts a page out of static
prerendering. Next requires a `<Suspense>` boundary around any component that calls it — skip the
split and the build fails with a CSR-bailout error.

```tsx
'use client';
import { Suspense } from 'react';

export default function ProductsPage() {
  return <Suspense fallback={null}><ProductsView /></Suspense>;
}

function ProductsView() {
  const query = useTypedSearchParams('/products', { onError: 'default' });
  query.page;    // number — ?page=2 really is 2 at runtime
  query.sort;    // 'price-asc' | 'price-desc' | 'name' | undefined
  query.inStock; // boolean | undefined — ?inStock=true really is true
}
```

`useTypedParams` and `useCurrentRoute` build on `usePathname` and need no boundary.

### 8.6 Check the tree against `app/`

`src/app/` decides which routes exist; the tree mirrors it by hand. `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next/check`
compares the two and reports drift in both directions. It reads the filesystem, so it is a **separate
entry point** — import it from a test or a script, never from application code.

```ts
// routes.test.ts
import { assertRoutesMatchAppDir } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next/check';
import { routes } from '@/routes';

test('the route tree matches src/app', () => {
  assertRoutesMatchAppDir(routes, 'src/app');
});
```

`findRouteDrift(routes, appDir, options?)` returns the same comparison as data —
`{ missingFromAppDir, missingFromTree, inSync }` — when you would rather report than throw.
`assertRoutesMatchAppDir` wraps it and throws `RouteDriftError`, whose `.report` is that object.

It reads Next's conventions the way Next does, so it never cries wolf. **Transparent** — no URL
segment of their own, but the walk still descends and pages underneath count: route groups
(`(shop)`) and parallel-route slots (`@modal`). `dashboard/@team/settings/page.tsx` is checked as
`/dashboard/settings`, because that is the route Next's own build emits for it — a page under a slot
is not exempt and must be declared like any other. **Skipped entirely** — no pathname of their own:
intercepting routes (`(.)`, `(..)`, `(...)`), private folders (`_folder`), and non-page files
(`route.ts`, `default.tsx`, `layout.tsx`, `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx`,
`template.tsx`).

Options: `pageExtensions` mirrors Next's own config (default `['tsx', 'ts', 'jsx', 'js']`), and
`ignore` takes **pathnames** — `'/coming-soon'`, or `'/admin/*'` for a route and its subtree — not
folder names. The skipped conventions above never need listing.

Opt-in on purpose: a check that blocks the build gets switched off, while one that fails in the
project's own test suite is tuned by the person who knows the app.

### 8.7 A tree declared elsewhere — `bindRoutes`

A tree declared with core's `defineRoutes` — in a shared package, framework-free so any app can
depend on it — gets this adapter's hooks and `TypedLink` from `bindRoutes`, without being declared a
second time:

```ts
import { bindRoutes } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next';
import { routes as shared } from '@acme/shop-routes';

export const routes = bindRoutes(shared); // same tree, paths and parsers; hooks added
```

Any core route tree works, including one returned by core's `attachMetadata`. When the app attaches
metadata as well, this package's own `attachMetadata(shared)(patch)` does both in one step.

A route that is in the tree but served elsewhere (a blog on another domain) is redirected with
`bindRoutes(tree, { useResolveHref })`. `useResolveHref` is a hook, so it can read the locale from
context. It returns `({ pathname, metadata, params, searchParams, hash }) => string | undefined`.
`push`, `replace`, `prefetch` and `TypedLink` use the returned URL, or the route's own href on
`undefined`, and `prefetch` skips absolute URLs. The library reads no metadata key. Return a stable
function (`useCallback`). With the option set, render `TypedLink` from client components. The
`/pages` entry's `bindRoutes` takes the same option.

### 8.8 The Pages Router — `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next/pages`

The same surface, backed by `next/router`: `defineRoutes`, `attachMetadata`, `bindRoutes`,
`TypedLink`, `useTypedRouter`, `useTypedParams`, `useTypedSearchParams`, `useTypedPathname`,
`useCurrentRoute`, `useCurrentRouteNode`, and the same core re-exports. It never loads the package
root, so `next/navigation` stays out of a Pages Router bundle — a Pages Router app imports only from
`/pages`.

```ts
import { bindRoutes } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next/pages';
import { routes as shared } from '@acme/shop-routes';

export const { TypedLink, useTypedRouter, useTypedParams, useTypedSearchParams, useCurrentRoute } = bindRoutes(shared);
```

Keys mirror `pages/`: `pages/products/[id].tsx` is `products: { '[id]': { _metadata: {} } }`, and
`pages/index.tsx` is `''`. The differences from the App Router:

- **The current route is `router.pathname`**, the page Next rendered, rather than a match of the URL,
  so rewrites cannot mislead it. `RouteMismatchError` works as in §8.4.
- **`<RouterReady>` replaces `<Suspense>`.** A page without `getServerSideProps` is prerendered with
  an empty `router.query`. `useTypedSearchParams` throws `RouteNotReadyError` until `isReady`;
  `useTypedParams` throws it only while a required segment is still missing (a statically optimized
  dynamic page before hydration — a `getStaticProps` page already has its segments). Wrap such
  components in `<RouterReady fallback={…}>`, or gate them on `useRouterReady()`. Never gate on
  `router.isReady` itself: on a statically rendered page without a query string it is `false` in the
  HTML and `true` on the first client render, which fails hydration. `getServerSideProps` pages need
  no boundary.
- **`push` / `replace` also take `shallow`**, and return `next/router`'s `Promise<boolean>`.
  `refresh()` re-navigates to the current URL, since the Pages Router has none of its own.

The drift check's counterpart is `assertRoutesMatchPagesDir(routes, 'src/pages')` /
`findPagesDirDrift`, reporting `{ missingFromPagesDir, missingFromTree, inSync }` and throwing
`PagesDirDriftError`. It reads `pages/` as Next does: every page file is a route, `index` serves its
folder, `_app`, `_document`, `_error`, `404`, `500` and `api/` at the root are skipped, and
`(group)`, `@slot` and `_folder` are literal segments — they are App Router conventions.

---

## 9. React Router 6/7 (library mode)

`@hyeonqyu/typed-router-react`. This section is React Router's **library mode**, the one where you
own the router configuration. Framework mode (`@react-router/dev`) is a different shape and is
covered in §9.4.

Same tree shape, plus the one thing React Router actually needs: an
element to render. The node's own page goes on `_metadata.element`; a wrapper goes on
`_metadata.layout`.

```tsx
// routes.tsx
export const routes = defineRoutes({
  home: { _metadata: { title: 'Home', element: <HomePage /> } },
  products: {
    _metadata: {
      title: 'Products',
      element: <ProductsPage />,
      searchParamsSchema: z.object({
        sort: z.enum(['price-asc', 'price-desc', 'name']).optional(),
        page: z.number().default(1),
      }),
    },
    '[id]': {
      _metadata: { title: 'Product detail', element: <ProductDetailPage /> },
      reviews: { _metadata: { title: 'Reviews', element: <ReviewsPage /> } },
    },
  },
  docs: { '[...slug]': { _metadata: { title: 'Docs', element: <DocsPage /> } } },
  // A route group becomes a pathless layout route: /profile and /orders share
  // AccountLayout without `(account)` ever appearing in the URL.
  '(account)': {
    _metadata: { layout: <AccountLayout /> },
    profile: { _metadata: { title: 'Profile', element: <ProfilePage /> } },
    orders: { _metadata: { title: 'Orders', element: <OrdersPage /> } },
  },
});

export const { TypedLink, useCurrentRoute, useCurrentRouteNode,
               useTypedParams, useTypedPathname, useTypedRouter, useTypedSearchParams } = routes;
```

### 9.1 Generate the router — the headline feature

`toRouteObjects()` builds React Router's `RouteObject[]` from the same tree. Hand-writing `<Route>`
elements or a `createBrowserRouter([...])` array beside the tree is exactly the parallel route list
this library exists to eliminate.

```tsx
import { createBrowserRouter, Navigate, RouterProvider } from 'react-router-dom';
import { routes } from './routes';

const router = createBrowserRouter(routes.toRouteObjects());
export default function App() { return <RouterProvider router={router} />; }
```

The result is ordinary data, so generating it costs you no control — nest it under your own shell,
add routes the tree knows nothing about, or filter it by feature flag:

```tsx
const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    element: <RootLayout />,
    errorElement: <ErrorPage />,
    children: [
      { index: true, element: <Navigate to="/home" replace /> },
      ...routes.toRouteObjects(),
      { path: '*', element: <NotFound /> },
    ],
  },
]);
```

`toRouteObjects()` rebuilds a fresh array on every call, so call it once and store the result before
handing it to `createBrowserRouter`. Inside an existing `<BrowserRouter>`, `<routes.TypedRoutes />`
is a thin wrapper rendering `useRoutes(routes.toRouteObjects())`.

Every React Router field on `_metadata` is forwarded untouched:

| in `_metadata` | becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `element` / `Component` / `lazy` | this node's page. If the node has children, it moves into an `index` route so it still renders at the exact path |
| `layout` | wraps the node's children through `<Outlet />`. On a childless node it stands in for `element` |
| `loader` / `action` / `shouldRevalidate` / `handle` / `middleware` | forwarded to this node's page |
| `errorElement` / `ErrorBoundary` / `HydrateFallback` / `hydrateFallbackElement` / `caseSensitive` / `id` | forwarded to this node's route, not its page |
| `[id]` key | `path: ':id'` |
| `[...slug]` / `[[...slug]]` key | `path: '*'` — params still report `slug`, not `*` |
| `(group)` key | a pathless layout route |

Confusing `element` with `layout` on a node that has children produces a route that renders nothing
at its own path — `element` is the page, `layout` is the wrapper.

A node whose `_metadata` names **no** page field at all — no `element`, `Component` or `lazy` —
still becomes a route: `{ path: 'about' }` with nothing to render. React Router renders `<Outlet />`
for an element-less route, which is empty when the node has no children, so `/about` matches and
shows nothing rather than falling through to a trailing `{ path: '*' }`. This is intended: the tree
declares information architecture, and a node may name a place without naming a page this router
draws. If such a path should 404, give the node a page or leave it out of the config.

### 9.2 Navigate and link

```tsx
function Actions() {
  const router = useTypedRouter();
  router.push('/home');
  router.push('/products/[id]', { params: { id: 42 } });
  router.push('/products/[id]/reviews', { params: { id: 42 }, hash: 'top' });
  router.push('/docs/[...slug]', { params: { slug: ['guide', 'intro'] } });
  router.replace('/products', { searchParams: { sort: 'price-asc', page: 2 }, state: { from: 'nav' } });
  router.back();
  router.forward();
  router.refresh(); // navigate(0) — re-runs loaders in a data router
}

<TypedLink href="/products/[id]" params={{ id: 42 }} className="link">Detail</TypedLink>
<TypedLink href="/products" searchParams={{ sort: 'price-asc', page: 2 }} hash="top" replace>Sorted</TypedLink>
```

React Router's navigate options (`state`, `preventScrollReset`, `flushSync`, `viewTransition`) sit
flat in the same argument object; `replace` and `relative` are derived by the library.

`TypedLink` takes **`href`**, not `to` — `to` is deliberately removed from the props type so the
same markup compiles against the Next.js adapter unchanged. Every other `Link` prop passes through.

`router.prefetch(...)` exists with the identical typed signature but is a **no-op** here: React
Router's library mode has no client-side prefetching. It is present purely so navigation code ports
between adapters. Do not build a perceived-performance story on it.

### 9.3 Read the current route, and use outside components

```tsx
function ProductDetail() {
  const { id } = useTypedParams('/products/[id]');   // { id: string } — or the segment's paramSchema output
  const { slug } = useTypedParams('/docs/[...slug]'); // { slug: string[] }
  const query = useTypedSearchParams('/products', { onError: 'default' });
  query.page; // number
  const { pathname, url, node, metadata } = useCurrentRoute();
  // on /products/42 → pathname: '/products/[id]', url: '/products/42'
}

// Loaders and actions cannot call hooks — use the methods on the same object.
export function productsLoader({ request }: { request: Request }) {
  const query = routes.parseSearchParams('/products', new URL(request.url).searchParams);
  return fetch(routes.buildHref('/products', { searchParams: { page: query.page } }));
}
```

Use `useTypedParams`, **not** React Router's `useParams()`. Because `[...slug]` compiles down to
React Router's `*`, `useParams()` hands you an anonymous `'*'` key; `useTypedParams` reads from
`routes.match(url)` instead, so the declared name survives. No Suspense boundary and no
client/server split here — `useTypedSearchParams` reads `useLocation().search` directly.

### 9.4 React Router 7 framework mode

`packages/react` accepts `react-router-dom ^7.0.0`, which includes framework mode
(`@react-router/dev`, an `app/routes.ts` config). What holds there is narrower than in library mode,
and the difference is worth stating exactly.

**`toRouteObjects()` does not apply.** It emits `element` / `Component` — React elements resolved at
runtime — while framework mode's `RouteConfigEntry` wants `file`, a module path resolved at build
time so the framework can code-split each route and generate its types. Same routes, units the other
cannot read. Do not try to feed one to the other.

**Everything else carries over**, because none of it ever depended on a router: `paths`,
`buildHref`, `match`, `parseParams`, `parseSearchParams`, `getNode`, `getMetadata` and `collected`
all work unchanged. Declare `file` on `_metadata` where library mode declares `element`, and build
the framework config from the tree:

```ts
// app/routes.ts
import { collectRoutes, parseSegment, splitPath } from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core';
import type { RouteConfig, RouteConfigEntry } from '@react-router/dev/routes';
import { routes } from '../src/routes';

const toFrameworkSegment = (segment: string): string => {
  const pattern = parseSegment(segment);
  if (pattern.kind === 'dynamic') return `:${pattern.name}`;
  if (pattern.kind === 'static') return pattern.value;
  return '*';                       // catchAll and optionalCatchAll
};

export default collectRoutes(routes.routes).flatMap((collected): RouteConfigEntry[] => {
  const file = collected.metadata?.file;
  if (typeof file !== 'string') return [];      // a place in the IA, not a page to build
  const path = splitPath(collected.path).map(toFrameworkSegment).join('/');
  return [path === '' ? { file, index: true } : { file, path }];
}) satisfies RouteConfig;
```

The root's empty key joins to a path of `''`, which is exactly what framework mode calls an index
route — hence the branch above.

**Import from `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core`, not the React adapter**, in framework mode. The
framework brings its own `<Link>` and its own hooks; the adapter's would be a second answer to a
question already answered. `routes.buildHref(...)` inside the framework's `<Link to>` gives you the
type checking without the duplication.

A complete, runnable version is `examples/react-router-framework-example`, pinned by
`tests/framework-mode.test.ts`.

---

## 10. Framework-free use

The tree is plain data, so `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core` gives the same declaration with no React
and no router — for scripts, servers, tests or a sitemap generator. `createRouteTree` is the
framework-agnostic half of `defineRoutes` (everything except `$types`); adapters wrap it and attach
their own hooks. Standalone, untyped helpers exist for when you hold a bare tree object rather than
a `defineRoutes` result:

```ts
import {
  buildHref, collectRoutes, matchRoute, parseSearchParams,
  collectRawSearchParams, toSearchParamsString,
  parseSegment, splitPath, isRouteGroup, children, searchParamKeys, METADATA_KEY,
} from '@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core';

buildHref('/products/[id]', { params: { id: 7 }, searchParams: { page: 2 } }); // untyped path
const collected = collectRoutes(routes.routes);
matchRoute(collected, '/products/7');
parseSearchParams(z.object({ page: z.number() }), { page: '4' });  // schema first, untyped return
collectRawSearchParams(new URLSearchParams('tag=a&tag=b'));        // { tag: ['a', 'b'] }
toSearchParamsString({ page: 2, tags: ['a', 'b'] });               // '?page=2&tags=a&tags=b'
toSearchParamsString({ f: { min: 1, max: 9 } });                   // '?f=%7B%22min%22%3A1%2C%22max%22%3A9%7D'
splitPath('/products/[id]').map(parseSegment);
isRouteGroup('(account)');                                          // true
children(routes.routes.products);                                   // children only, no `_metadata`
METADATA_KEY;                                                       // '_metadata'
```

Prefer the methods on `routes` in application code — the standalone versions accept any string and
give up the type checking that is the whole point.

---

## 11. Mistakes to avoid

Roughly in order of how often they occur.

1. **Hand-writing a URL.** `'/products/42'`, `` `/products/${id}` ``, or a `PATHS` constants file.
   Use `buildHref` / `push` / `TypedLink` with the declared pattern.
2. **Putting path params in `searchParams`.** The 1.x shape. `params` fills the pathname,
   `searchParams` fills the query string.
3. **Assuming any nested key is navigable.** Only nodes with `_metadata` are destinations; add
   `_metadata: {}` to promote an organisational node.
4. **Inventing a provider or generics.** No `<AppRoutesProvider>`, no `useAppRoutes()`, no
   `defineRoutes<Meta>({...})`. The only curried form is `defineRoutes.withMeta<M, C>()({...})`.
5. **Using `to` on `TypedLink`**, or nesting the destination in an object. It is a flat `href` plus
   sibling `params` / `searchParams` / `hash`, in both adapters.
6. **Ignoring the default `onError: 'throw'`.** A hand-edited URL crashes the render, on either half
   of it. Pass `{ onError: 'default' }` where users can edit the query string or the path.
7. **Calling `useTypedSearchParams` on a schema-less route.** The type is `never`, so it compiles
   clean and hands you raw strings at runtime.
8. **Forgetting the `<Suspense>` boundary** around a Next.js component calling
   `useTypedSearchParams`.
9. **Feeding Next 15's `searchParams` straight in.** Await it and strip the `undefined` values.
10. **Expecting `match()` to be narrowed or validated.** `path` is `string`, `params` a loose record
    of raw text — `match` runs no schema. Feed it to `routes.parseParams(match.path, match.params)`.
11. **Treating `useTypedPathname()` as the live URL.** It is the declared pattern; the live URL is
    `useCurrentRoute().url`.
12. **Mixing the two type families.** `Pathname<typeof routes>` (routes object) vs
    `RoutePaths<TTree>` / `CurrentRoute<TTree>` (raw tree). Mixing them does not give you `never` —
    it either trips TS2589 or invents paths like `'/routes/products'`.
13. **Rendering `getMetadata(path).title` unresolved** when declared as a function. Call
    `resolveMetadata(meta, context)`, which resolves only the four built-in resolvable keys.
14. **Making `zod` a hard dependency** or narrowing a public type to `z.ZodType`.
15. **Hand-writing the React Router config** instead of `toRouteObjects()`.
16. **Reading catch-all params with React Router's `useParams()`**, which reports `'*'`.
17. **Importing from `-core` in an app.** Import from the single adapter package — except in
    React Router's framework mode, where core *is* the right import (§9.4).
18. **Expecting `(group)` to appear in a URL**, or writing `'/(account)/profile'`.
19. **Mutating the tree at runtime.** It is structurally frozen.
20. **Expecting a path param to be a number without declaring it.** A segment reads back as `string`
    until it declares a `paramSchema` (§6.1) — and that schema is bare (`z.number()`), goes on the
    `'[id]'` node itself, and is inherited rather than repeated on nested routes.
21. **Passing a pathname the component is not rendered under**, to `useTypedParams` or
    `useCurrentRouteNode`. It is checked against the route the URL matched and throws
    `RouteMismatchError`; an ancestor is fine, anything else is not (§8.4).
22. **Reaching for `useCurrentRouteNode<'/products/[id]'>()`.** The type argument was never checked
    against anything. Pass the pathname as a value instead.
23. **Feeding `toRouteObjects()` to React Router's framework mode.** It emits `element`; framework
    mode wants a build-time `file` (§9.4).
24. **Emitting any 1.x API.** See §12.

---

## 12. Upgrading from 1.x

2.0 is a breaking rewrite. The tree you already wrote survives almost unchanged; what changes is
how you declare it and how you navigate. 1.x had four unfixable problems: dynamic segments were
invisible to the type system (`push('/products/[id]')` navigated to that literal string), routes
without a schema accepted anything, `useTypedSearchParams` never actually ran the schema, and
`useCurrentRouteNode()` returned `undefined` on every dynamic route.

| 1.x | 2.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `createAppRoutes<M, C>()({...})` | `defineRoutes({...})` |
| `AppRoutesProvider` / `useAppRoutes()` | not needed — `routes` is a module-level object |
| `_types.AppRoutesPathname` | `Pathname<typeof routes>` or `typeof routes.$types.pathname` |
| `_metadata.href` | derive from the tree, or `routes.buildHref(...)` |
| `_metadata.name` | dropped; metadata is inferred per node |
| `getPathnameFromNode(node)` | `routes.match(url)` / `routes.paths` |
| `@hyeonqyu/typed-router-core/routes.utils` subpath | the main entry |
| `push(path, { searchParams: { id, page } })` | `push(path, { params: { id }, searchParams: { page } })` |
| `<TypedLink href={{ pathname, searchParams }}>` | `<TypedLink href={pathname} searchParams={...}>` |
| `useTypedPathname()` → the live URL | → the declared pattern; use `useCurrentRoute().url` for live |

Never emit a 1.x API. Expect new compile errors where 1.x was silently permissive — a missing `id`,
or search params on a route that declares no schema. Those are the bugs 2.0 exists to catch.

---

## 13. API reference

```ts
defineRoutes(tree)                                   // → TypedRoutes<TTree>
defineRoutes.withMeta<TMetadata, TContext>()(tree)   // → TypedRoutes<TTree>, shared contract
```

On the returned `routes` object, in **every** package:

| member | signature | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `routes` | `TTree` | the declared tree, structurally frozen |
| `paths` | `readonly RoutePaths<TTree>[]` | every navigable pathname |
| `collected` | `readonly GetCollectedRoute<TTree>[]` | `{ path, segments, node, metadata }`, one union member per route — `metadata` stays typed while enumerating |
| `getNode(path)` | `GetRouteNode<TTree, TPath>` | `undefined` at runtime for an unknown path |
| `getMetadata(path)` | `GetRouteMetadata<TTree, TPath>` | literal types preserved; not resolved |
| `match(url)` | `RouteMatch \| null` | loose `path: string`, `params: Record<string, string \| string[]>` — raw text, no schema run |
| `buildHref(path, args?)` | `string` | `args` omittable when the route needs nothing |
| `parseSearchParams(path, raw, options?)` | schema **output** type | `raw`: record, `URLSearchParams`, or entries iterable |
| `parseParams(path, raw, options?)` | `PathParamsOutput<TPath, TTree>` | runs each segment's `paramSchema` over `match().params`; undeclared segments pass through |
| `$types` | `{ tree; pathname }` | type-only carrier; `{}` at runtime |

**On `-next` and `-react` additionally:** `TypedLink`, `useTypedRouter` (`push` / `replace` /
`prefetch` / `back` / `forward` / `refresh`), `useCurrentRoute`, `useCurrentRouteNode(pathname?)`,
`useTypedParams(pathname, options?)`, `useTypedPathname`, `useTypedSearchParams` — all client-only.
The pathname `useTypedParams` takes, and the one `useCurrentRouteNode` optionally takes, are checked
against the route the live URL matched; a mismatch throws `RouteMismatchError` (§8.4). `-next/pages`
has the same members backed by `next/router` (§8.8). `-react` adds
`toRouteObjects()` and `<TypedRoutes />`, and its `prefetch` is a no-op while `refresh` is
`navigate(0)`.

**Exported functions:** re-exported by **every** package — `buildHref`, `children`, `matchRoute`,
`collectRoutes`, `parseSearchParams`, `searchParamKeys`, `parsePathParams`, `toSearchParamsString`, `resolveMetadata`,
`resolveMetadataValue`, `isRouteGroup`, `METADATA_KEY`, `SearchParamsParseError`,
`PathParamsParseError`, `RouteMismatchError`, `assertRouteMatches`, `isSameOrAncestorRoute`.
**Core only**
(not re-exported by the adapters) — `createRouteTree`, `mergeRouteMetadata`, `collectRawSearchParams`,
`parseSegment`, `splitPath`. **Each package its own** — `defineRoutes`, `attachMetadata`; `bindRoutes` on `-next` and `-next/pages`. **`-next/pages` only** — `RouteNotReadyError`, `RouterReady`, `useRouterReady`. **React only** — `toRouteObjects`, `toReactRouterSegment`.

**Exported types:** `Pathname`, `SearchParams`, `Params`, `RouteNodeOf`, `RouteMetadataOf`,
`CollectedRouteOf`, `RouteArgs`, `RouteChildren`, `AttachedTree`, `MetadataPatch`, `MetadataPatchWithMeta`, `PathParams`, `PathParamsOutput`, `RouteMatch`, `RoutePaths`,
`RouteMetadata`, `BuiltinMetadata`, `MetadataValue`, `ResolvedMetadata`, `ResolvableMetadataKey`,
`UseCurrentRouteNode`, `AnySchema`, `SearchParamKeysSchema`, `SearchParamsErrorMode`,
`PathParamsErrorMode`, `RawPathParams`, `PathParamSchemas`,
`CurrentRoute<TTree>`, `TypedRoutes<TTree>`, `TypedLinkProps`, `NavigateArgs`, `NavigateArgsTuple`,
`NavigateOptions`.

**`@hyeonqyu/typed-router-next/check`** — a separate, Node-only entry point (it reads the
filesystem, so it never belongs in application code): `assertRoutesMatchAppDir(routes, appDir,
options?)`, `findRouteDrift(routes, appDir, options?)`, `RouteDriftError`, and the types
`RouteDriftReport`, `FindRouteDriftOptions`, `RoutesLike` — and for the Pages Router
`assertRoutesMatchPagesDir`, `findPagesDirDrift`, `PagesDirDriftError`, `PagesDirDriftReport`,
`FindPagesDirDriftOptions`. Nothing here is re-exported from the main
entry, and there is no React Router equivalent — `toRouteObjects()` makes one unnecessary.

The adapters re-export only a **subset** of core: `RawSearchParams`, `ParseSearchParamsOptions`,
`ParsePathParamsOptions`, `BuildHrefArgs`, `CollectedRoute`, `GetRouteNode`, `GetCollectedRoute`, `RouteArgsTuple`,
`SearchParamsInput` / `SearchParamsOutput`, `RouteTreeInput` and `-next`'s `TypedRouter` are **not**
among them — import those from core, or use `ReturnType<typeof routes.useTypedRouter>`.

---

## 14. Runnable examples

Four apps in the repository. `next-example` and `react-example` declare the *same* tree, and their `Nav.tsx` and
`RouteInspector.tsx` are identical line for line apart from the Next copies' `'use client'`
directive and their header comments — proof that the API is identical across adapters. Every page
prints what the library resolved for the live URL with the runtime `typeof` beside it, so the type
claims are visible rather than asserted. Run `yarn workspace next-example dev` (:3000),
`yarn workspace react-example dev` (:5173) or
`yarn workspace react-router-framework-example dev` (:5174).

- `examples/next-example/src/routes.ts` — the Next.js declaration
- `examples/next-pages-example/src/routes.ts` — the Pages Router: a tree declared with core in
  `src/shared/routes.ts`, bound with `bindRoutes` from `-next/pages`, with `<RouterReady>` around its
  statically optimized pages (`yarn workspace next-pages-example dev`, :3001)
- `examples/react-example/src/routes.tsx` — the React Router declaration, `element` per node
- `examples/react-example/src/App.tsx` — `toRouteObjects()` nested under a hand-written shell, with
  an index redirect and a `*` catch-all the tree knows nothing about
- `examples/react-example/src/components/PermissionNav.tsx` — a menu built from `routes.collected`
  and `resolveMetadata`, filtered by the `accessible` built-in against a role picker
- `examples/react-router-framework-example/app/routes.ts` — framework mode: the tree turned into
  `RouteConfigEntry[]`, and the answer to what `toRouteObjects()` can and cannot do there (§9.4)
